newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU, Boeing near collision on merger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU, Boeing near collision on merger.

text.p: Boeing Co appeared on Thursday on a collision course with the EU over its planned merger with McDonnell Douglas, although the U.S. aircraft maker seemed to be holding the door ajar for more talks and the U.S. president spoke of the risks of a trade war.
"Our discussions with the Commission have been suspended but they may resume at any time," Boeing's vice-president for European affairs Jim Frank told Reuters.
But a spokesman for the EU's Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said it would take a miracle to break the deadlock, indicating that any move would have to come from Boeing.

"It is going to be tough for Boeing to come up with something in time unless there is a miracle," the spokesman told a news briefing, reiterating that the Commission planned to take its final decision on whether to block the deal on July 23.
A majority vote would be enough.
President Bill Clinton said in Washington the European Union and the United States would "probably" avoid a trade war over the issue.
"There's an orderly process for our handling of this and I think we'd better let the orderly process play itself out before we talk ourselves into a trade war," he said.

French President Jacques Chirac said on a visit to Brussels on Thursday he fully backed the European Commission's plan to block the merger as an increasingly tense confrontation developed between the two sides.

The Commission has the power to block the deal if Boeing does not meet its concerns, especially over exclusive supply contracts signed with three large U.S. airlines and the perceived risk that defence subsidies could spill over to the commercial aircraft sector.
Were Boeing to ignore an EU ruling against it, the Commission could fine it up to 10 percent of its turnover and fine any European companies doing business with the U.S. aviation giant.
Commission sources said the EU could also seize any new planes delivered to Boeing in Europe.

The committee of anti-trust experts from the EU's 15 states agreed unanimously on Wednesday that the $14 billion merger should be blocked, saying Boeing had not met the Commission's concerns that the deal would harm fair competition in Europe.
Were Boeing to make a new offer, the Commission is unlikely to reject it despite having said that the deadline for submitting any changes to the deal has now passed.
Asked whether the Commission would refuse a Boeing offer if it was made on July 22, the spokesman said:
"I don't know. I don't see how we could still inform the (experts) advisory committee. It's unthinkable how we could do that in such a short time, but I don't know."

The spokesman repeated that the Commission must take its final decision next week, although the official deadline is July 31, because of strict rules on clearing the text of the ruling, translating it into the official EU languages and getting it signed.
Companies have in the past successfully challenged controversial Commission decisions in the European Court of Justice on the grounds of procedural irregularities.
The committee of antitrust experts, aware that a ban could cause a huge political row with the United States, has urged the Commission to explore the negotiation route.

Members of the U.S. Congress on Wednesday reacted strongly to the European experts' negative advice, accusing the European Commission of defending the interests of French-based European aerospace consortium Airbus, Boeing's only global rival, and warning it could lead to a trade war.

"The sole true reason for the European Commission's criticism and imminent disapproval of the merger is to gain an unfair competitive advantage for Airbus, a government-owned aircraft manufacturer," said Republican Senator Slade Gorton, from Boeing's home state of Washington.

Van Miert reacted promptly. "Van Miert wishes to recall firmly that the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas file was reviewed strictly under the Merger Regulation and that the Commission's analysis was founded only on facts and tangible figures, not on some 'political motive'," he said in a statement.
The 20 commissioners' aides specialising in competition affairs will meet later today to discuss the draft decision prepared by Van Miert's staff.
